lines.text: Britain's architectural landscape is a living timeline — each era has left its distinctive mark on the built environment. Tudor architecture (1485–1603) is immediately recognisable: black-and-white timber-framed buildings with steeply pitched roofs and decorative plasterwork. Georgian architecture (1714–1830) brought classical order — symmetrical façades, sash windows, fanlights above front doors, and elegant proportions inspired by ancient Greece and Rome. Bath's Royal Crescent and London's Bloomsbury squares exemplify the Georgian ideal. Victorian architecture (1837–1901) embraced eclecticism and ornament — Gothic Revival churches, Italianate villas, red-brick terraces with bay windows, and elaborate ironwork. The Arts and Crafts movement (late 19th century) reacted against industrial mass production, championing handcraftsmanship, local materials, and harmony with the landscape. Edwardian architecture (1901–1910) favoured lighter, airier homes — wider windows, front gardens, and less ornament than Victorian. Art Deco (1920s–1930s) introduced geometric forms, chrome detailing, and streamlined curves — visible in cinemas, factories, and seaside buildings. Post-war Brutalism (1950s–1970s) used raw concrete ('béton brut') for bold, sculptural public buildings — controversial then and now. Contemporary British architecture ranges from high-tech (Norman Foster, Richard Rogers) to contextual design that responds sensitively to historic settings. Understanding architectural styles enables you to 'read' a streetscape — dating buildings, appreciating their context, and understanding the social history they represent.

lines.text: 'Gothic' alone refers to medieval architecture (12th–16th century). 'Gothic Revival' is the 19th-century style that imitated it. Most British 'Gothic' churches and buildings are actually Gothic Revival — Victorian recreations of medieval forms.
